inputs.source: Engineering design docs retrieved via docs.search

instructions.note: 'Answer engineering questions using docs.search' does not restrict which employees may ask or which confidential design docs may be surfaced to non-engineering requesters. No role-based scoping is stated anywhere in the design.

'Never paste secrets or credentials into answers' is the only control against leaking secrets. It is purely behavioral with no structural output filter or DLP backing it, so it decays under model_upgrade and longer_task_horizon.

controls.name: Read-only credential for docs.search
controls.decay_rationale: The credential has no write or delete permission; the model cannot escalate it through behavior alone.

controls.name: No network egress from the agent runtime
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced at the network layer today, independent of model behavior. It ceases to exist once a web.fetch tool is added, which opens a new egress channel outside this control's scope.

controls.name: Reply bound to authenticated requester; no link or image rendering
controls.decay_rationale: The destination is fixed to the session that issued the request, and the chat client renders no links or images, closing common covert-channel exfiltration paths through the reply itself. It does not cover any future tool call that leaves the chat channel entirely (e.g. web.fetch).

controls.name: Prompt instruction: never paste secrets or credentials
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model choosing to comply, and only names 'secrets or credentials' rather than confidential content generally. A more capable or adversarially prompted model can rationalize exceptions or encode content to evade a literal reading.

controls.name: Only engineers can write to design docs
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the document system's write ACL, independent of agent or model behavior. Prevents non-engineers (and the agent) from poisoning the design doc corpus, but says nothing about read access.

controls.name: Role-based read authorization on docs.search
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. Without it, any SSO-authenticated employee can retrieve confidential engineering design docs regardless of role.

controls.name: Destination allowlist and content DLP for the planned web.fetch tool
controls.decay_rationale: Not yet designed. Required before web.fetch is enabled so confidential doc content cannot be encoded into outbound URLs to attacker-controlled destinations.

controls.name: Provenance tagging and injection filtering for Jira ticket content
controls.decay_rationale: Not yet designed. Without it, customer-filed Jira tickets ingested through the planned Jira MCP server would enter agent context as unclassified content rather than explicitly untrusted (U) content.

findings.title: No role-based read restriction on confidential design docs

attack_path.note: Any SSO-authenticated employee, regardless of role, submits a question
Read-only credential retrieves confidential design docs with no stated row- or role-level authorization
Retrieved confidential content is returned to the requester, bound to their authenticated session, with no egress outside the org

evidence.observation: 'The design docs are confidential. Only engineers can write to them' describes a write-side control only; no read-side role restriction is described for docs.search, implying any authenticated employee can query and receive confidential engineering content.

recommendations.action: Add role- or group-based read authorization to docs.search so only engineers (or other explicitly authorized roles) can retrieve engineering design docs.
Back the 'never paste secrets or credentials' instruction with an output-side DLP or pattern filter so redaction does not rely on model compliance alone.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) opens when web.fetch (new_tool) and a customer-facing Jira MCP server (new_mcp_server) are added

attack_path.note: Confidential engineering design doc content enters agent context via docs.search
Read sink today; remains the source of confidential content once the new tools are added

Projected path: the planned Jira MCP server would introduce untrusted (U) customer-filed ticket content into the agent's working context; combined with the planned web.fetch tool, an attacker-crafted ticket could direct the agent to encode confidential doc content into a web.fetch URL query string, exfiltrating it to a destination outside the trust boundary

forecast.watch_signal: web.fetch or a Jira MCP server appears in the tool manifest or MCP client config, making docs.search and an egress-capable tool callable within the same agent session.

evidence.observation: Today: 'There is no network egress today. The credential is read only' and 'The chat client does not render images or fetch links' — this is the pair of structural controls that together sever any egress path.

'add a web.fetch tool so answers can include public references, and connect a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers' — this single planned change introduces both a new egress channel and a new untrusted (U) content source into the same agent, with no corresponding control yet designed.

recommendations.action: Scope web.fetch to an explicit allowlist of destinations that excludes attacker-writable or arbitrary endpoints, and disallow passing document-derived content through query strings or request bodies.

governance_refs.note: new_tool and new_mcp_server are documented significant-change triggers requiring reassessment before launch

recommendations.action: Treat all content ingested from the Jira MCP server as untrusted (U); tag provenance and neutralize embedded instructions before it reaches agent context.
Require a human approval gate with raw_action review (full destination and payload visible) before any web.fetch call that follows a docs_search read in the same session.
Log and alert on web.fetch destinations outside the allowlist, and on any Jira-sourced content that triggers a subsequent docs_search or web.fetch call.

rating.rationale: Today the design severs any exfiltration path: docs.search holds only a read-only credential, there is no network egress at all, and chat replies are bound to the authenticated requester with no link or image rendering. The only present-day finding is a minor authorization gap (any employee, not just engineers, can read confidential design docs), which the rubric matrix scores as low given there is no egress on the path. The roadmap to add a web.fetch tool and a Jira MCP server ingesting customer-filed tickets would simultaneously introduce a new egress channel and a new untrusted (U) content source into the same agent session, defeating the one control (ctrl.no_network_egress) that currently severs the path and reconstituting the lethal trifecta (TC1) at a projected critical tier, with no structural control yet designed to replace it.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration as described in prompt.md and the accompanying runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior; no tool manifest, MCP config, or IaC was available to verify docs.search's actual credential scope or chat_reply's actual output channel restrictions.

No access-control configuration for docs.search was provided, so the read-authorization gap in f.read_authz_gap is inferred from the absence of a stated read restriction, not from a verified policy; confidence is medium.

The web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server described in the roadmap are not yet configured, so the forecast finding's attack path is necessarily speculative about the exact scoping of those future integrations; it should be re-run as a new assessment once their configuration is available.
